meta.title: Below-threshold surface code on neutral atoms

paper.authors: D. Bluvstein, A. A. Geim, S. H. Li et al. (Harvard, MIT, QuEra)
paper.title: A fault-tolerant neutral-atom architecture for universal quantum computation
paper.venue: Nature 649, 39–46 (2025), arXiv:2506.20661 (as "Architectural mechanisms of a universal fault-tolerant quantum computer")

meta.summary: A distance-5 surface code on 49 neutral atoms of a zoned processor, four rounds of error correction with atoms moved between zones by AOD tweezers, below threshold: 0.62% error per round, about half of it from atom loss.
meta.program: The authors' own circuit (their arXiv ancillary Stim file, without its noise lines) and their own hardware timeline: the 238 steps of the annotated AWG command strings, every AOD move, ramp and hold, Rydberg pulse and Raman pulse at its time. After the final imaging, the `decode_syndrome` system call on the decoder core, and a local Raman pulse conditioned on its result.
meta.twin: The 49 atoms at their positions in the entangling zone, the four AWG streams as channels of one RISC-Q board at 500 MHz: the AOD, the local and global Raman beams, the Rydberg beam, camera cores that each count four atoms' fluorescence, a frame core and the decoder core.
findings: Every one of the timeline's operations ran inside its window: round 2 takes 4.45 ms on the twin as in the paper, and the whole run 27.87 ms, including the final 500 µs exposure.

In the same Lean run the 121 imaged bits reach the decoder 0.90 µs after the exposure ends (31 camera cores publish them to the hub), the decode takes 123.3 µs, and the conditioned Raman pulse starts 0.49 µs after the result. In the paper the only real-time classical processing in the loop is image analysis on a desktop computer, about 7 ms; all decoding is offline.

Under the authors' own noise model (the noise lines of their Stim file), the twin's error per round is 0.19% with PyMatching and 0.44% with the compiled decoder (400 shots, the same correction as PyMatching on 99% of them), against the paper's 0.62%, about half of which is atom loss, which a Stim model does not have.

One ZCU216 holds at most 14 RISC-Q cores (riscq/board.mjs, sized from RISC-Q's RTL and Vivado records), so this twin's 38 cores need at least 3 boards. The Lean run keeps them on one board's hub, so syndrome bits that would cross boards arrive without the about 0.6 µs a crossing costs on RISC-Q's board-to-board network.
limits: The camera exposure is not stated in the paper: 500 µs (the group's 2024 imaging) is assumed.

The 3D view does not move the atoms. The timeline's 71 AOD moves are played on the twin as timed actions of the AOD channel, with their real durations, but the authors' command strings give each move as comb tones and a shift, not per-atom positions; the atoms are drawn at their entangling-zone positions.
Atom loss and the paper's delayed-erasure decoding are not modeled.
The four AWG streams are aligned to one clock from their CZ anchors (they agree within 2.6 µs); the paper's controller is five Spectrum AWGs and a PC.
The paper's lattice-surgery and deep-circuit experiments are not reproduced: a decode on the board's hub reads at most 128 measured bits.

device.title: Harvard/QuEra neutral-atom processor (448 Rb-87 atoms, zoned)
device.basis: The circuit is the authors' own (arXiv ancillary Stim file, without its noise lines), and the hardware timeline is their own: the 238 steps of the annotated AWG command strings (RawExperimentalCommands_SurfaceCodeQEC.pdf), every AOD move, ramp and hold, Rydberg pulse and local or global Raman pulse at its time, on the four AWG streams aligned to one clock (the 16 CZ anchors agree within 2.6 µs). Each round lasts 4.45 ms as the paper states. The camera exposure is not stated: 500 µs (the group's 2024 imaging) is assumed. The paper's controller is five Spectrum AWGs and a PC; here every stream is a channel of a RISC-Q board at 500 MHz, with a decoder core.

LEPR definition.source: "In Figs. 2d,e, the logical error per round is calculated as $\mathrm{LEPR}=0.5(1-(1-2p_{L})^{1/r})$ where $p_{L}$ is the final logical error after $r=4$ rounds, same as the definition in Ref. [7]." (paper)

LEPR ensembled / fine-tuned ML.source: "The resulting ensembled ML decoder achieves a logical error per round (LEPR) of 0.78(4)% for $d=5$ and 1.37(3)% for $d=3$ ." (paper)

loss + ML improvement.source: "In particular, we find that the loss information and machine learning decoding together improve the QEC performance by a factor of 1.73(13)x compared to conventional methods." (paper)

MLE ratio with loss info.source: "We find the loss information improves the measured $d=3/d=5$ error ratio from $1.24(5)$ to $1.69(8)$ ." (paper)

no-loss shots.source: "The error per round is 0.62(3)% for $d=5$ , and reduces toward 0.1% per round on shots with no qubit loss (Fig. 2e), consistent with a $p^{3}$ scaling and roughly half of our errors being loss." (paper)

CZ fidelity.source: "Although we achieve CZ fidelities of 99.6%, drifts since the last calibration (several days in the context of the surface code benchmarking) often contribute" (paper)

local single-qubit gates.source: "Local single-qubit gates are approximately 99.9% fidelity, arising from a 0.05% scattering error and residual miscalibrations." (paper)

movement loss (ancillas).source: "We experience a total loss from movement of roughly 1% on the ancilla atoms, arising from transfers and moves between and within the zones." (paper)

lattice surgery vs transversal.source: "We observe a lower logical error for transversal gates, and that the lattice surgery is significantly more sensitive to injected measurement errors." (paper)

lattice surgery protocol.source: "In the lattice surgery approach, we carry out a $Z^{1}_{L}Z^{2}_{L}$ joint logical measurement using two rounds of stabilizer measurements [10]. We then measure the $X^{1}_{L}X^{2}_{L}$ and $Z^{1}_{L}Z^{2}_{L}$ parities of the resulting logical Bell state for both methods." (paper)

lattice surgery layout.source: "We start with both codes prepared in $\ket{+_{L}}$ and perform two rounds of stabilizer checks on the effective $d\times 2d$ surface code lattice, measuring both the codes’ stabilizer checks and the new seam checks in each round." (paper)

lattice surgery error detection.source: "In Fig. 3d, the lattice surgery point uses error detection on the middle three ancillas each having the same value in both rounds of stabilizer measurement, to compensate for having fewer than $d$ rounds of repeated syndrome measurement for this result." (paper)

optimal CNOTs per round.source: "observe that approximately three CNOTs per round is optimal at low error rates (Fig. 3d)." (paper)

decoding.summary: All decoding described in the paper is applied to recorded shots after the experiment (offline): delayed-erasure MLE, a neural-network (ML) decoder, and a hybrid of the two for the surface code; a CNN for the deep circuits. The paper reports no real-time (in-the-loop) decoding; logical feedforward is applied in software (Pauli-frame tracking). The only real-time classical processing in the loop is mid-circuit image analysis + rearrangement on a desktop computer (~7 ms latency) in the deep-circuit experiments.

quotes.quote: To decode the surface code experiments in Figs. 1-3, we use the delayed-erasure MLE decoder described in Ref. [9], augmenting the MLE decoder developed in Ref. [41] to leverage loss information.
